clinicalScope: Epidemiology in low‑resource, East African hospital settings
subject: Public health
summary: Epidemiology is the science of who gets sick, why, and how many. In East Africa it guides ward rounds, test choices, and prevention plans when labs are scarce.

sections.p: Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of disease in populations, informing prevention and control. In low‑resource hospitals it shapes clinical priorities and resource allocation.
Common endemic diseases drive admissions: malaria, HIV, TB, diarrhoeal disease, and sickle cell crises. Burden is measured by incidence, prevalence, and mortality rates.
b: Sickle cell crisis: 15% of paediatric admissions

sections.p: Determinants include socioeconomic status, environmental exposure, genetics, and behaviour. Risk factors are often modifiable.
b: Malaria: stagnant water, lack of nets

sections.p: Routine data come from hospital records, community health workers, and national health information systems. Interpretation must account for under‑reporting and diagnostic gaps.
Screening targets high‑risk groups; prevention focuses on vaccination, vector control, and health education.
b: TB screening: symptom questionnaire, sputum microscopy

sections.p: Interventions must be affordable, culturally acceptable, and sustainable. Implementation science guides adaptation.
b: Task shifting: nurses for malaria diagnosis
Mobile phone reminders for medication adherence
Supply chain management for drugs and diagnostics

sections.p: Policy decisions rely on epidemiological evidence to allocate limited resources and set priorities.
Equity ensures vulnerable groups receive care; community engagement improves uptake.
Continuous monitoring of intervention coverage and outcomes is essential for quality improvement.
b: Coverage indicators: % of pregnant women with ITNs

sections.p: Clinicians use epidemiology to decide which tests to order, which empiric therapies to start, and when to refer.
b: Empiric malaria treatment when microscopy unavailable
Empiric TB therapy in high‑prevalence settings
Prioritising HIV testing in febrile patients

sections.p: Data gaps, diagnostic delays, and cultural barriers limit accuracy.
Examiners test understanding of disease patterns, risk assessment, and application to clinical scenarios.

whenToSeekHelp: HIV‑related opportunistic infection with high fever

faq.q: What is the difference between incidence and prevalence?
faq.a: Incidence is new cases over a period; prevalence is all existing cases at a point.

faq.q: Why is malaria still common in East Africa?
faq.a: Persistent breeding sites, insecticide resistance, and gaps in net coverage.

faq.q: How can I use epidemiology in a ward round?
faq.a: Assess local disease patterns to guide empiric therapy and investigations.

exam: What is the most likely diagnosis for a 5‑year‑old with fever, vomiting, and dehydration in a rural clinic? — Malaria (high endemicity) vs. bacterial sepsis; choose malaria empirically if microscopy unavailable.
In a patient with chronic cough and weight loss, which test is most useful in a low‑resource setting? — Sputum microscopy for TB; explain limitations of GeneXpert.
Why is IPTp recommended for pregnant women in malaria‑endemic areas? — Prevents maternal anaemia and low birth weight; explain mechanism.
When should you refer a patient with suspected typhoid fever? — If persistent fever >7 days, or signs of perforation; explain referral criteria.
Explain the role of community health workers in malaria surveillance. — They collect data, distribute nets, and educate; discuss impact on case detection.
How does under‑reporting affect malaria control programmes? — Leads to under‑estimation of burden; discuss mitigation strategies.
What is the WHO target for ITN coverage in sub‑Saharan Africa? — 80% of households; explain how to achieve it.
Why is HIV testing mandatory in all febrile adults in high‑prevalence settings? — Early detection improves outcomes; discuss ethical considerations.
Describe the steps to implement a syndromic management protocol for STIs in a primary clinic. — Screening, empiric therapy, partner notification; explain rationale.
What are the key indicators for evaluating a TB programme? — Treatment success rate, default rate, sputum conversion; explain each.
